Motion to Intervene

Normally, a lawsuit involves the plaintiffs (who bring the suit), and the defendants (whom the suit is brought against). Sometimes, a person who is not a party to a lawsuit in progress wants to become a party. Such a party must file a Motion to Intervene. Generally, to be admitted into the lawsuit, the intervenor must have an interest in the subject matter of the original suit.

A motion to intervene in a case in Federal Court is addressed by Rule 24 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. It provides in part that:

(a) Intervention of Right. Upon timely application anyone shall be permitted to intervene in an action: (1) when a statute of the United States confers an unconditional right to intervene; or (2) when the application claims an interest relating to the property or transaction which is the subject of the action and the applicant is so situated that the disposition of the action may as a practical matter impair or impede the applicant's ability to protect that interest, unless the applicant's interest is adequately represented by existing parties.

Or view on goog earth here.

At first it looks like a composite between summer and winter photos maybe, but then you see what appears to be mountainous terrain (in the snow) over a glacier or shallow waterway (from summer image).

Because it is a composite. It usually takes many passes of a satellite or multiple satellites to take images at a decent resolution 1-15 meters per pixel. Sometimes things happen that prevent the satellites from being able to return to get clear images like Orbit, Weather other projects. So when the satellite returns to capture the missing imagery it could be a different season.

Now lets talk about the other artifacts like geographical features not lining up and very obvious boxes. Land based imagery is processed VIA orthorectification. Essentially what this does is takes a flat image, georeferences it to the curvature of the earth may it be in the WGS1984 datum or some other coordinate system then warps the images so the image is truthful to the ground. What I mean by truthful is that the GPS coordinates will be accurate if you click on random spots on the image. Sometimes during this process the algorithm gets a little funky and images become really warped. Sometimes you can fix this sometimes you can't and have to live with the best image you can get till a new dataset is acquired. After the orthorectification process the very large image, usually a GeoTIFF is then tiled (Turned into a bunch of smaller images usually 256x256 pixels) to make the image load better inside of web browsers. Pay attention to when maps load in google maps. The will load in square chunks or become clearer in square chunks. You are literally watching the tiles load for the larger orthorectified image.
